detective.q: Genesis 9 curses Ham and his descendants with dark skin.
detective.why: Genesis 9:25 curses Canaan, Ham's son, and says nothing about skin color. The racial reading was added many centuries later.

detective.q: In 1662 Virginia made a child enslaved or free according to the mother's status.
detective.why: Virginia's 1662 act (partus sequitur ventrem) is in the colony's statutes. It meant children of enslaved women, including those fathered by enslavers, were born enslaved.

detective.q: Margaret Sanger, founder of the group that became Planned Parenthood, supported eugenics.
detective.why: Her writings and speeches show it, and Planned Parenthood itself acknowledged it in 2020.

detective.q: Planned Parenthood was founded to exterminate Black Americans.
detective.why: The record does not support it. Sanger opposed abortion in her lifetime, and Planned Parenthood did not provide abortions until about 1970. The real, documented abuses are forced sterilizations by states and federal programs.

detective.q: After Bacon's Rebellion (1676), Virginia's leaders deliberately used race to divide poor white and Black workers.
detective.why: The laws that followed are documented. How deliberate the strategy was is debated by historians (see Edmund Morgan and his critics).

detective.q: The U.S. Public Health Service watched hundreds of Black men go untreated for syphilis for 40 years.
detective.why: The Tuskegee study ran from 1932 to 1972. A federal panel reviewed it, and President Clinton apologized in 1997.

detective.q: Modern American policing grew directly out of slave patrols.
detective.why: Slave patrols are well documented and shaped Southern policing. Northern departments also grew from other models, such as the London police, so how direct the line is remains debated.

detective.q: The Book of Enoch explains where the different races came from.
detective.why: 1 Enoch tells of fallen angels (the Watchers) and their giant children. It has no teaching about race. Some modern groups have built race myths on it.

detective.q: The Vatican formally repudiated the “Doctrine of Discovery” in 2023.
detective.why: Two Vatican departments issued a joint statement on March 30, 2023, rejecting the doctrine.

detective.q: Racism was a consequence of slavery, not its original cause.
detective.why: This was Eric Williams's argument in Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Many historians agree; others stress older prejudices that existed before Atlantic slavery.

modules.title: Before race: where the fear came from
modules.short: There is no ancient secret. Race was built, mostly between 1450 and 1700, to justify taking land and people, and the fear behind it was fear of losing power.
modules.intro: People often ask why the targeting of Black, Brown and Native people has lasted so long, and whether some forgotten origin explains it. The record gives a clearer answer: modern race is recent, it was written into law on purpose, and it has been defended by whatever argument was handy, including scripture and science.

sections.h: The ancient world sorted people differently
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
Slavery is ancient, but for most of history it was not based on skin color. Greeks, Romans, Egyptians, Africans, Arabs and Europeans enslaved people taken in war, sold for debt, or born to enslaved mothers, and enslaved people came from every region. The English word slave itself comes from Slav, because so many Eastern Europeans were enslaved in the Middle Ages.

Historian Frank Snowden showed that Greek and Roman writers described Africans with curiosity and sometimes admiration, without the idea of a fixed racial ranking.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The idea that some people are naturally meant to be owned was spelled out step by step:

  • 1452–1455: Pope Nicholas V's bulls Dum Diversas and Romanus Pontifex authorized Portugal's king to conquer “Saracens and pagans” and reduce them to perpetual slavery. Portugal's African slave trade grew under them.
  • 1493: Inter caetera gave Spain lands “discovered” in the Americas. These bulls became the Doctrine of Discovery, which the U.S. Supreme Court adopted in Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823) to deny Native nations full ownership of their land. The Vatican repudiated the doctrine in 2023. The Supreme Court has not.
  • 1662: Virginia ruled that a child follows the condition of the mother, so children of enslaved women, including children of their enslavers, were born enslaved.
  • 1667–1705: Virginia declared that baptism does not free a slave (1667), that killing an enslaved person during “correction” was not a felony (1669), banned interracial marriage (1691), and gathered everything into the 1705 slave codes. France's Code Noir (1685) did the same for its colonies.

sections.label: debated
sections.body:
In 1676, Bacon's Rebellion brought white indentured servants and enslaved Africans together in an armed revolt against Virginia's government. In the decades that followed, Virginia's laws gave poor white people small privileges (freedom dues, the right to bear arms, the right to strike a Black person) while taking rights away from all Black people, free or enslaved.

That the laws changed is documented. Historian Edmund Morgan argued that the elite used race on purpose to keep poor white and Black people from uniting again. Others think the shift had more to do with the falling cost of enslaved Africans compared with English servants. Most agree the effect was the same.

sections.h: The practice came first, the ideas followed
sections.label: debated
sections.body:
In 1944 the Trinidadian historian Eric Williams wrote that “slavery was not born of racism: rather, racism was the consequence of slavery.” Ibram X. Kendi's Stamped from the Beginning (2016) traces the same pattern over five centuries: racist ideas were developed to defend policies that were already profitable.

Thomas Jefferson, who enslaved more than 600 people over his life, offered Black inferiority “as a suspicion only” in his Notes on the State of Virginia (1785). Within decades, “scientists” were measuring skulls to prove it (see module 5).

sections.h: What the fear was really about
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The fear was real. It was fear of revolt, of revenge, and of losing power at the ballot box:

  • Haiti, 1791–1804: enslaved people overthrew French rule and founded the first free Black republic. France later forced Haiti to pay 150 million francs (reduced to 90 million) for its own freedom, a debt Haiti paid off over about 120 years.
  • Nat Turner's rebellion, 1831: afterward, Virginia and other states tightened bans on teaching Black people to read and on Black preachers and gatherings.
  • Reconstruction, 1867–1877: Black men voted and held office, and South Carolina's lower house had a Black majority. White-supremacist violence ended it, including the 1898 coup in Wilmington, North Carolina, where an elected biracial government was overthrown by force.
  • “Replacement”: Madison Grant's The Passing of the Great Race (1916) warned that white Americans were being outbred. It helped pass the 1924 immigration quotas. The same fear, renamed the “Great Replacement,” was cited by the killers in El Paso (2019) and Buffalo (2022).

sections.h: How scripture was used, and misused
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The “Curse of Ham.” In Genesis 9:20–27, Noah curses Canaan, Ham's son, to be a servant. The text says nothing about skin color or Africa. Linking the curse to dark skin came much later and was spread by interpreters across several traditions. By the 1800s it was a standard pro-slavery argument in American pulpits.

The “Slave Bible.” In 1807 a British missionary society printed Select Parts of the Holy Bible, for the Use of the Negro Slaves. It cut most of the Old Testament, including the Exodus story of freedom from slavery, and kept passages like “Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters.”

Scripture was also the strongest weapon against slavery: enslaved people sang of Moses and Exodus, and abolitionists from Frederick Douglass to the Black church built their case on it.

sections.h: The Book of Enoch and modern race myths
sections.label: belief
sections.body:
1 Enoch is an ancient Jewish book that is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church; fragments were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the Letter of Jude (verses 14–15) quotes it. It tells how angels called the Watchers came to earth, taught forbidden knowledge, and fathered giants (the Nephilim of Genesis 6). It contains no teaching about race.

Modern movements have still built race stories on Genesis and Enoch. We describe them so you can recognize them, not because they are true:

  • Christian Identity “two-seedline” theology, a white-supremacist doctrine claiming Jews and people of color descend from the serpent or from “pre-Adamic” races.
  • The Nation of Islam's story of Yakub, which teaches that a scientist named Yakub created white people thousands of years ago.
  • Some Hebrew Israelite groups teach that Black, Hispanic and Native Americans are the true Israelites and that others are cursed.

These stories mirror each other: each claims race is ancient, fixed and cosmic. The historical record shows the opposite: race is recent, made by people, and can be unmade.

modules.title: Science as a weapon: medicine, eugenics and reproductive control
modules.short: Scientific racism, medical experiments, and the forced sterilization of tens of thousands of Americans, plus what the evidence does and doesn't show about Planned Parenthood.
modules.intro: When religion could no longer justify slavery and segregation, science was asked to. This module covers what was done in medicine's name, much of it within living memory, and separates the documented record from claims that go beyond it.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1758 Carl Linnaeus divided humans into varieties and gave each a temperament: Europeans “governed by laws,” Africans “governed by caprice.” In the 1830s–40s Samuel Morton measured skull sizes to rank races, and in 1854 Josiah Nott and George Gliddon's Types of Mankind argued the races were separate species, a book widely used to defend slavery. None of it holds up: modern genetics finds more variation within any so-called race than between them.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
• J. Marion Sims, 1845–1849: the “father of modern gynecology” developed his surgery by operating repeatedly, without anesthesia, on enslaved women including Anarcha, Betsey and Lucy. New York City removed his Central Park statue in 2018.
  • Tuskegee, 1932–1972: the U.S. Public Health Service followed about 600 Black men in Alabama, 399 of them with syphilis, without telling them their diagnosis and without treating them, even after penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s. It ended only when a whistleblower went to the press. President Clinton apologized in 1997.
  • Henrietta Lacks, 1951: cells taken from her cancer without her knowledge became the HeLa line used in labs worldwide. Her family reached a settlement with one company in 2023.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In Buck v. Bell (1927) the Supreme Court upheld forced sterilization (“Three generations of imbeciles are enough”). It has never been overruled. More than 60,000 people were sterilized under laws in 32 states. Early victims were mostly poor white people labeled “feebleminded”; after the 1950s, in the South especially, they were increasingly Black women.

  • North Carolina's Eugenics Board sterilized about 7,600 people from 1929 to 1974. In 2013 it became the first state to pay survivors.
  • Fannie Lou Hamer was sterilized without consent in 1961 while having a tumor removed. She called it a “Mississippi appendectomy,” a common experience among Black women in the South.
  • The Relf sisters, ages 12 and 14, were sterilized at a federally funded clinic in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1973. Their lawsuit led to federal consent rules.
  • Native women: a 1976 federal audit (GAO) found 3,406 sterilizations by the Indian Health Service in just four of its twelve areas from 1973 to 1976, many with inadequate consent.
  • Puerto Rico: by 1965 about a third of mothers had been sterilized, under programs encouraged by U.S. and island officials.
  • California sterilized about 20,000 people from 1909 to 1979, and nearly 150 women in state prisons from 2006 to 2010; a 2014 state audit found consent rules were broken.
  • Immigration detention: a 2022 bipartisan U.S. Senate investigation found that women at the Irwin County center in Georgia underwent excessive and often unnecessary gynecological procedures.

sections.label: debated
sections.body:
Margaret Sanger founded the American Birth Control League in 1921, which became Planned Parenthood in 1942. She supported eugenics, as many Progressive-era reformers did, and spoke to a women's auxiliary of the Ku Klux Klan in 1926. In 2020 Planned Parenthood of Greater New York removed her name from its Manhattan clinic over her eugenics ties.

In 1939 her federation started the “Negro Project” to bring birth control to the rural South. W.E.B. Du Bois and Mary McLeod Bethune supported it. In a letter about it, Sanger wrote: “We do not want word to go out that we want to exterminate the Negro population, and the minister is the man who can straighten out that idea if it ever occurs to any of their more rebellious members.” Historians disagree about that sentence. Most read it as worry that rumors would sink the project, not as a secret plan; critics read it as revealing.

sections.h: “Planned Parenthood was founded to exterminate Black Americans”
sections.label: belief
sections.body:
This claim, common in political campaigns, goes beyond the record. Sanger opposed abortion in her lifetime; she promoted contraception. Planned Parenthood did not provide abortions until about 1970. The documented coercion against Black, Native and Latina women came mainly from state eugenics boards and government-funded programs, not from a hidden plan inside one organization.

This site takes no position on abortion. It documents coercion: anyone, on any side, who wants to end it should know where it actually happened.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
CDC abortion surveillance reports show the abortion rate among Black women is roughly four times the rate among white women. Research from the CDC and the Guttmacher Institute links this to higher rates of unintended pregnancy, which in turn follow from unequal access to contraception and health care, from poverty, and from well-earned distrust of the medical system.

The same unequal system shows up elsewhere: Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at about two and a half to three times the rate of white women (CDC), a gap that holds even for college-educated women.

modules.title: Burned, flooded and taken: the communities America destroyed
modules.short: Black Wall Street in Tulsa and dozens of other Black, Brown and immigrant communities that were burned, driven out, flooded, seized or bulldozed, plus how gentrification continues the pattern.
modules.intro: Again and again, when Black communities built wealth, voted or simply grew, they were attacked: burned by mobs, driven off their land, flooded for dams, seized for parks and beaches, or bulldozed for highways. Each loss wiped out homes and businesses that would have passed wealth down to the next generation. This module tells those stories, and they are all on the map.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In the early 1900s, Greenwood was home to about 10,000 Black residents. Its main street had hotels, theaters, groceries, doctors' and lawyers' offices, churches, two newspapers and a hospital. Oklahoma's segregation laws kept Black dollars inside the district, and they circulated there. Booker T. Washington is credited with calling it the “Negro Wall Street.” O.W. Gurley, J.B. Stradford and other Black entrepreneurs built it on land they owned.

May 31–June 1, 1921. A Black teenager, Dick Rowland, was arrested after a white elevator operator accused him of assault. A newspaper story inflamed the city. Black World War I veterans went to the courthouse to stop a lynching, and a white mob, many of them deputized by officials, invaded Greenwood. Over about 18 hours they burned 35 city blocks, including about 1,256 homes. The 2001 Oklahoma commission found that airplanes were used in the attack and estimated that 100 to 300 people were killed. About 6,000 Black residents were held in internment camps.

Afterward. Insurance companies denied claims under “riot” clauses, and the city tried to rezone the burned district so it couldn't be rebuilt. No one was ever prosecuted. Residents rebuilt anyway. Then, in the 1960s and 1970s, urban renewal and Interstate 244 cut through Greenwood again.

Still unresolved. The 2001 state commission recommended reparations; none have been paid by the state. Searches for mass graves at Oaklawn Cemetery began in 2020, and in 2024 one set of remains was identified as C.L. Daniel, a World War I veteran. Also in 2024, the Oklahoma Supreme Court dismissed the last survivors' lawsuit. In January 2025 the U.S. Justice Department called the massacre a civil rights crime of unparalleled magnitude, but said no one left alive could be prosecuted.

sections.h: Burned: a pattern, not an accident
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
Tulsa was one of many. The death tolls below are estimates, and many are disputed because officials undercounted. The pattern is clear: a mob, often set off by an accusation against a Black man or by Black voting, organizing or success, followed by fire.

  • Colfax, Louisiana, 1873: an estimated 62–153 Black men killed defending a courthouse after an election. The Supreme Court then let the killers go (U.S. v. Cruikshank, 1876).
  • Wilmington, North Carolina, 1898: the only successful coup on U.S. soil. The Black newspaper was burned and at least 60 people were killed.
  • Atlanta 1906, Springfield 1908, Slocum 1910: each sparked by rumors or accusations. Springfield led directly to the founding of the NAACP.
  • East St. Louis, 1917: about 6,000 people left homeless after white workers attacked Black workers.
  • Red Summer, 1919: violence in more than two dozen cities. In Elaine, Arkansas, Black sharecroppers trying to form a union were massacred, with estimates from about 100 to several hundred dead.
  • Ocoee, Florida, 1920: Black residents tried to vote. The entire Black community was burned out.
  • Rosewood, Florida, 1923: a white woman's accusation led to a whole town being burned. In 1994 Florida became the first state to pay reparations for racial violence.
  • Philadelphia, 1985: police dropped a bomb on the MOVE house; 11 people died, including 5 children, and 61 homes in a Black neighborhood burned.

Chinese immigrants were attacked the same way: in Los Angeles in 1871, in Rock Springs, Wyoming, in 1885, and in Tacoma, Washington, which expelled its entire Chinese population that year.

The link to today is direct. Many of these attacks started with one false accusation to the authorities, which is the harm the CAREN Act targets.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
• Forsyth County, Georgia, 1912: after a lynching, night riders drove out about 1,100 Black residents. White neighbors took over their farms. The county stayed almost entirely white for 75 years.
  • Sundown towns: historian James Loewen documented hundreds, possibly thousands, of towns that kept Black people out by violence or law, often after driving out those already there (see the old laws tracker).
  • Seneca Village, New York, 1857: the city's largest community of Black property owners was taken by eminent domain and razed to build Central Park.
  • Bruce's Beach, California, 1924: a Black-owned beach resort was seized by the city of Manhattan Beach. In 2022 Los Angeles County returned it to the Bruce family's descendants, an early example of returning stolen land.
  • Chavez Ravine, Los Angeles, 1950s: Mexican American neighborhoods were cleared for public housing that was never built; the land became Dodger Stadium.
  • Black farmland: around 1910, Black farmers owned roughly 15 million acres. Most of it is gone. It was lost to violence, to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's discrimination in loans (settled in Pigford v. Glickman, 1999), and to forced sales of “heirs' property” passed down without a will.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
• Oscarville, Georgia: its Black residents were driven out in 1912. The land was later flooded to create Lake Lanier (Buford Dam, 1956).
  • The Great Mississippi Flood, 1927: Black residents were held in levee camps under armed guard and forced to work on the levees, while white residents were evacuated.
  • Vanport, Oregon, 1948: Oregon's largest Black community, built for wartime shipyard workers, was destroyed when a dike broke. Survivors were pushed into Portland's Albina neighborhood, which was later cut up by a freeway and then gentrified.
  • The Lower Ninth Ward, New Orleans, 2005: levee failures during Hurricane Katrina flooded this mostly Black neighborhood. The Road Home rebuilding program based grants on pre-storm home values, so Black homeowners in undervalued neighborhoods got less; the state and HUD settled a lawsuit in 2011. Much of the neighborhood was never rebuilt.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The Housing Act of 1949 and the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 sent billions of federal dollars to clear “blight,” a label usually given to the same neighborhoods the redlining maps had marked red. Hundreds of thousands of families were displaced, people of color far out of proportion to their numbers. James Baldwin called it “Negro removal.”

The list of Black business districts and neighborhoods cut apart is long: Rondo in St. Paul (I-94), Overtown in Miami (I-95), Tremé in New Orleans (I-10 over Claiborne Avenue), Hayti in Durham, Black Bottom and Paradise Valley in Detroit (I-375), Sweet Auburn in Atlanta, the Hill District in Pittsburgh, the Fillmore in San Francisco, Albina in Portland, and Greenwood in Tulsa a second time.

Some of this is now being undone. The 2021 infrastructure law created a Reconnecting Communities program, Detroit is replacing I-375 with a boulevard, and Minnesota's transportation department apologized for Rondo in 2015.

sections.label: debated
sections.body:
Gentrification is when higher-income, usually whiter residents and investment move into a lower-income neighborhood, raising rents and property values. That it happens, and that many historically Black neighborhoods have changed rapidly, is documented. A 2019 study by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition estimated that gentrification displaced more than 135,000 Black and Hispanic residents from 2000 to 2013, concentrated in cities like Washington, Portland and Seattle.

What's debated is how much gentrification itself pushes people out, as opposed to normal moving. Some economists find that longtime residents of gentrifying areas are not much more likely to move than residents elsewhere. Others find that those who do leave are pushed to poorer neighborhoods, and that rising taxes, evictions and the loss of churches and businesses damage the community even for those who stay.

The link to the CAREN Act is well documented: as neighborhoods change, longtime residents are reported for doing what they've always done. In 2018 a white woman called police on a Black family barbecuing at Oakland's Lake Merritt. In 2019 a new resident's complaint about go-go music in Washington's Shaw neighborhood sparked #DontMuteDC, and the city made go-go its official music.

What helps: community land trusts that keep homes affordable for good, property-tax relief for longtime owners, tenant protections, and “right to return” policies like Portland's N/NE Preference Policy (2015), which gives families pushed out of Albina priority for new affordable housing.

modules.title: Policing and the 911 call
modules.short: From slave patrols and vagrancy laws to the weaponized 911 call, and what the data shows about who gets stopped and hurt.
modules.intro: The CAREN Act is about one specific harm: calling the police on someone because of their race. This module shows where that harm comes from and why a phone call can be dangerous.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: From South Carolina's 1704 law onward, Southern colonies and states organized slave patrols: white men who rode at night, stopped Black people, demanded passes, searched slave quarters and whipped people found without permission. Every white person was expected to help police enslaved people.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: After emancipation, many Southern patrol duties passed to new city police and sheriffs. How direct the line is from patrols to modern policing is debated: Northern departments (Boston 1838, New York 1845) grew mostly from London's model and from controlling immigrants and labor. Historians agree that in the South, the job of controlling Black movement carried over.

sections.h: Black Codes, vagrancy laws and convict leasing
sections.label: documented
sections.body: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery “except as a punishment for crime.” Southern states immediately passed Black Codes making it a crime for Black people to be unemployed, to walk at night, or to “loiter.” Those arrested were leased to plantations, mines and railroads, often dying at higher rates than under slavery. Convict leasing lasted in Alabama until 1928.

sections.h: An accusation could be a death sentence
sections.label: documented
sections.body: Many lynchings began with an accusation from a white person. In 1955 Carolyn Bryant's account of an encounter in a Mississippi store led to the murder of 14-year-old Emmett Till. (In a 2017 book, historian Timothy Tyson reported that she later admitted parts of her account were untrue; her family disputes this. That detail is debated.) The lesson the CAREN Act builds on is older than any single case: when the person called about is Black, the police response can be deadly.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In 2018 and 2020, videos showed white callers phoning police about Black people barbecuing (Oakland), waiting in a Starbucks (Philadelphia, where two men were arrested), selling water (San Francisco) and birdwatching (Central Park). San Francisco passed the CAREN Act in 2020, following Oregon's 2019 law and California's AB 1775.

The data backs up the videos. In San Francisco, only about 1% of “suspicious person” calls in the past year led to an arrest, citation or report. The federal Police-Public Contact Survey (2020) found that Black people who had contact with police were nearly three times as likely as white people to experience threats or use of force.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Cities are sending trained responders instead of armed police to many calls. Eugene, Oregon's CAHOOTS program has done so since 1989. A 2022 study in Science Advances found that Denver's STAR program reduced reports of the low-level crimes it targeted. A federal CAREN Act adds the other half: a consequence for using the police as a weapon.

modules.title: The path forward
modules.short: What has actually worked, and where you fit in.
modules.intro: None of this history was inevitable, and none of it is permanent. Each of these remedies has a track record, and each has a role for you.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: San Francisco's CAREN Act, Oregon's 2019 law and California's AB 1775 give targets a remedy. A federal version would extend that everywhere. Read and improve the draft, then ask your lawmakers to introduce it.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Programs like CAHOOTS (Eugene) and STAR (Denver) send medics and counselors to calls that don't need police. Ask your city council whether yours has one.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Truth commissions (South Africa 1996, Greensboro 2004–2006, Canada 2008–2015) and memorials like EJI's National Memorial for Peace and Justice in Montgomery put the record where everyone can see it. Teaching these modules is part of that work.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving Japanese American who had been incarcerated. North Carolina and Virginia have compensated sterilization survivors. Evanston, Illinois, began housing reparations in 2021, California's Reparations Task Force issued its final report in 2023, and H.R. 40 would create a federal commission. Whether and how to do more is debated; the precedents are documented.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Segregation-era language still sits in some codes and deeds. Volunteers can verify old laws and deliver repeal requests, and many states now let homeowners strike covenants from their deeds.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: District attorneys, sheriffs and city councils decide how the police are used, and they are often elected by a few thousand votes. Register, check your registration, and vote in local elections.
